title: Exact Clifford Optimality for Two-Sided Locally Randomized Classical Shadows
authors: Xiaotian Nie, Tao Zhang, Yadong Wu, Linghui Chen
abstract: Entangling measurements can reduce the statistical cost of learning many-body correlations. We study Pauli strings with full support on a specified $k$-qubit region using classical shadows with two independent, uniformly random product single-qubit Clifford layers around a controllable unitary acting on that region, followed by computational-basis readout. In this architecture, we prove that a circuit $U_*$ of two collective Pauli rotations attains the exact minimum squared shadow norm over all Clifford choices of the controllable unitary for every $k\geq1$, namely $C_k^{\rm opt}=4\cdot 9^k/(3\cdot 5^k+3^k-6)$ for odd $k$ and $C_k^{\rm opt}=4\cdot 9^k/(3\cdot 5^k-3^k+2)$ for even $k$. The asymptotic optimum $(4/3)\cdot(9/5)^k$ establishes Wu et al.'s exponential base as optimal and improves their prefactor from $2$ to $4/3$. For $1\leq k\leq6$, exact rational certificates prove that the same optimum holds over the entire unitary group $\mathrm U(2^k)$, including all non-Clifford unitaries, within the same measurement architecture. These finite-size results motivate the conjecture that $U_*$ is optimal over all unitaries for arbitrary $k$ within this architecture.
summary: This paper rigorously determines the minimum statistical cost for estimating many-body Pauli correlations using a specific randomized quantum measurement scheme. The authors prove that a simple, structured circuit $U^*$ achieves this theoretical minimum for all $k$, significantly improving previous asymptotic estimates. The work establishes strong optimality results for small systems and provides deep mathematical tools for analyzing quantum measurement resource bounds.
main_problem: The paper determines the exact minimum statistical cost (squared shadow norm) required to estimate many-body Pauli correlations on a $k$-qubit region using a specific two-sided locally randomized Clifford measurement architecture.
main_result: The authors prove that a simple circuit $U^*$ of two collective Pauli rotations achieves the exact minimum shadow norm for all $k \ge 1$ within the Clifford measurement setting, and this optimum extends to the entire unitary group $U(2^k)$ for small $k$.
method: The analysis relies heavily on symplectic linear algebra, quadratic forms on $\mathbb{F}_2^{2k}$, and deriving necessary constraints from the Choi state representation to establish rigorous upper and lower bounds on the measurement cost.
model_or_system: The system involves estimating Pauli strings (observables) acting on a $k$-qubit region within a larger quantum system. The measurement protocol uses a two-sided randomized Clifford measurement structure: $bU = bR_2 bUg bR_1$.
key_observables: Squared shadow norm ($C_k$), Pauli weight, and the score function ($S_k$) which quantifies the sampling cost.
important_parameters: The number of qubits in the region ($k$), and the asymptotic scaling factor $(9/5)^k$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the measurement architecture is restricted to two-sided locally randomized Clifford gates, although the results for small $k$ extend optimality to the full unitary group $U(2^k)$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the classical shadow tomography protocol, compare the exact statistical costs for full-support estimation using $U^*$ versus other circuits, and show asymptotic cost ratios for sliding-block measurements.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general framework using symplectic tools, deriving necessary constraints from the Choi state, providing exact rational certificates for small $k$ (up to $k=6$), and finally analyzing asymptotic behavior for sliding-block measurements.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous, finite-size optimality proofs for quantum state tomography protocols, which is crucial for designing resource-efficient quantum measurements in quantum computing and quantum information theory.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the classical shadow tomography proto- col for a Pauli string operator acting on a subsystem, following Ref. [24]. The protocol comprises a global Clifford unitary bUg (blue block) sandwiched between two layers bR1 and bR2 of random single-qubit Clifford rotations (pink blocks) applied to the subsystem. Filled and open circles denote nonidentity and identity factors of the propagated Pauli string, respec- tively.

FIG. 2. Exact output-size distributions for a full-support in- put on k = 50 qubits. The random Clifford and contractive distributions reproduce the comparison in Ref. [24]; U∗adds the two-rotation construction of this work. Each bar height is the probability π(m) at an integer output size m. Translucent bars are centered at m/k; different widths distinguish over- lapping bars, including the coincident odd-m probabilities of bUct and U∗. The full-size peak is approximately 1/2 for bUct and 1/4 for U∗. All values are exact combinatorial probabili- ties, with no sampling or smoothing.

FIG. 3. Exact statistical costs for full-support estimation on a k-qubit block, from the closed-form Pauli weights. The U∗curve is the Clifford optimum of Theorem 2 for every k; dashed lines show the asymptotic coefficients 2 and 4/3. Black rings at 1 ≤k ≤6 mark the points also certified optimal over bUg ∈U(2k), including non-Clifford unitaries, in the same measurement architecture (Theorem 7). Lines connect integer values of k as a guide to the eye.

FIG. 4. Uniformly shifted blocks, illustrated at k = 6. The target occupies the same six filled sites in both rows. Each measurement block contains k sites; open sites carry identity factors of the target observable. One offset aligns the target with a block. The other k −1 offsets split it between neighboring blocks; the example has k1 = 2 and k −k1 = 4. The region size, target length, and block size all equal k here. The chain continues beyond the displayed sites.

FIG. 5. Exact statistical costs for a length-k contiguous tar- get measured with uniformly shifted k-site blocks, from the closed-form Pauli weights. The curves evaluate the two stated constructions, with asymptotic coefficients 32/19 and 128/99. The figure does not assert optimality among sliding protocols. Lines connect integer values of k as a guide to the eye.
